title: Steel structures
summary: IS 800:2007 is a limit state code, and its two partial factors (1.10 for yielding, 1.25 for rupture) explain most of the design expressions. Section classification comes before everything else, because a slender section buckles locally before reaching yield and no plastic reserve exists. For connections, learn the bolt and weld capacity expressions and the geometric limits on pitch and edge distance — they are the most reliably examined items in the subchapter.

sections.heading: Limit state design and section classification
sections.body:
**IS 800:2007** replaced the older working stress code, and its structure follows the limit state pattern:

> **Design strength = characteristic strength / γ_m**

| Partial factor | Value | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **γ_m0** | **1.10** | **Yielding** and buckling |
| **γ_m1** | **1.25** | **Ultimate (rupture)** |
| γ_mb | 1.25 | Bolts — bearing type |
| γ_mw | 1.25 (shop) / 1.50 (site) | Welds |

**Rupture takes the larger factor because it is a brittle failure mode with no warning**, whereas yielding is ductile and gives visible deformation first. The same reasoning explains the higher factor for **site** welds than shop welds — less controlled conditions, more variable quality.

**Properties of structural steel:** **E = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm²**, **G = 0.769 × 10⁵**, **μ = 0.3**, **α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C**, **unit weight 78.5 kN/m³**.

**Grades (IS 2062):**

| Grade | f_y (N/mm²) | f_u (N/mm²) |
|---|---|---|
| **E250 (Fe 410)** | **250** | **410** |
| E300 (Fe 440) | 300 | 440 |
| E350 (Fe 490) | 350 | 490 |
| E410 (Fe 540) | 410 | 540 |

**Section classification — done FIRST, before any capacity is computed.** Four classes, by the **width-to-thickness ratio** of the compression elements:

| Class | Name | Behaviour | Can it be used in plastic design? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Plastic** | Forms a plastic hinge and **sustains the rotation** required for a mechanism | **Yes** |
| **2** | **Compact** | Reaches **M_p** but cannot sustain the rotation | No — elastic analysis only |
| **3** | **Semi-compact** | Reaches **first yield (M_y)** only | No |
| **4** | **Slender** | **Buckles LOCALLY before reaching yield** | No; capacity must be reduced |

The limits are expressed against **ε = √(250/f_y)**, so a higher-grade steel has **tighter** slenderness limits — because yield is reached at a higher stress, at which local buckling is more likely.

**Why classification comes first.** A **slender** section's capacity is governed not by its material strength but by the **local buckling of its plate elements**, so applying the yield-based expressions would overestimate it. And plastic analysis, which relies on **moment redistribution** through successive hinges, is valid **only for Class 1 sections** — a Class 3 or 4 section cannot rotate at constant moment, so no redistribution occurs. That is why a question about plastic design always turns on section class.

**Design bending strength:**

| Class | M_d |
|---|---|
| **1 and 2 (plastic, compact)** | **β_b Z_p f_y / γ_m0**, with β_b = 1.0 |
| **3 (semi-compact)** | **Z_e f_y / γ_m0** |
| 4 (slender) | Based on an effective section |

subject also to **M_d ≤ 1.2 Z_e f_y/γ_m0** for a simply supported beam — a cap that prevents excessive deformation at service load.

**Laterally unsupported beams** must additionally be checked for **lateral–torsional buckling**: a deep narrow beam can buckle sideways and twist long before its section capacity is reached. The design bending strength is then reduced by a **bending stress reduction factor χ_LT**, which depends on the **effective length between lateral restraints**. That is why beams are laterally restrained by the slab, by secondary beams or by bracing — and why an unrestrained deep beam is far weaker than its section modulus suggests.

**Shear capacity:**

> **V_d = A_v f_yw / (√3 γ_m0)**

with **A_v** the shear area — for a rolled I-section, **the WEB area (h × t_w)** alone. The **√3** comes from the von Mises criterion, which puts the shear yield stress at f_y/√3.

The web-only assumption reflects reality: because the flanges are wide and the web narrow, shear stress **jumps** at the flange–web junction and the web carries roughly **95%** of the total shear at nearly uniform stress. The associated limit states are therefore **web buckling and web crippling**, checked at concentrated loads and supports, and countered by **bearing and intermediate stiffeners**.

sections.heading: Tension and compression members
sections.body:
**Tension members** have **three** possible failure modes, and the design strength is the **least** of them:

| Mode | Design strength |
|---|---|
| **Yielding of the gross section** | **T_dg = A_g f_y / 1.10** |
| **Rupture of the net section** | **T_dn = 0.9 A_n f_u / 1.25** |
| **Block shear** | T_db, along a path of shear and tension planes |

**Why the net section takes the larger safety factor.** Rupture at a bolt hole is a **brittle** local failure, so γ_m1 = 1.25 applies, together with the **0.9** factor. Yielding of the gross section is ductile, so γ_m0 = 1.10 suffices. The two expressions can be compared to see which governs: for a member with few holes the gross yielding usually governs; with many holes or a high f_u/f_y ratio, rupture does.

**Net area** deducts the bolt holes: **A_n = (b − n d_h) t** for a plate, using the **hole** diameter (bolt + 2 mm clearance). Where holes are staggered, the **critical path** must be found by trying the possible zig-zag failure lines, with an allowance for the stagger.

**Block shear** is a mode that a candidate might not think of: a **block of material tears out** along a combination of shear and tension planes through the bolt group, rather than the member rupturing across its net section. It governs where the bolt group is close to the member end, and the remedy is a larger end distance or more spread-out bolts.

**Shear lag** affects **angles and tees connected through one leg only**: the load enters through the connected leg and does not spread fully into the outstanding leg, so the effective area is less than the net area. IS 800 handles this with a reduction factor based on the outstanding and connected leg widths — and it is why a **double angle** connected on both sides of a gusset is substantially more efficient than a single angle.

**Compression members.** The design strength is

> **P_d = A_e f_cd**

where **f_cd** is the design compressive stress, obtained from the **non-dimensional slenderness** and the **buckling class**.

**IS 800 uses four buckling curves (classes a, b, c, d)** with an **imperfection factor α**, following the Perry–Robertson approach. The class depends on:

| Factor | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Section shape** | Affects the distribution of residual stress |
| **Axis of buckling** | A rolled I-section has different classes about its two axes |
| **Manufacturing process** | **Hot-rolled, welded or hollow** sections carry different **residual stresses** from fabrication |
| Thickness | Thicker plates cool more unevenly |

The **residual stress** explanation is the substance: welding and uneven cooling leave locked-in stresses of significant magnitude, so parts of the section yield earlier than the applied stress alone would suggest, reducing the effective stiffness at the moment buckling begins. Four curves rather than one formula is the code's way of accounting for that quantitatively.

**Effective length** depends on the end restraints:

| End conditions | L_e |
|---|---|
| Both ends **effectively held in position and restrained against rotation** | **0.65 L** |
| Held in position, one end restrained against rotation | 0.80 L |
| **Held in position at both ends, restrained against rotation at neither** | **1.0 L** |
| Held in position at one end only | 1.2 – 2.0 L |

Note that IS 800's practical values (0.65 rather than the theoretical 0.5) acknowledge that a real "fixed" end is never perfectly rigid.

**A column buckles about the axis of MINIMUM radius of gyration**, so **k_min** governs — and for a rectangle or an I-section that is the weak axis. Using the strong-axis value overestimates capacity dangerously.

**Slenderness limits (IS 800 Table 3):**

| Member | Maximum λ |
|---|---|
| **Compression member carrying loads** | **180** |
| Compression member resisting only wind or seismic | 250 |
| Bracing designed to resist tension only | 350 |
| **Tension member** | **400** |

**Tension members have a limit too**, which seems counter-intuitive since a tension member cannot buckle. The reason is **serviceability**: an over-slender tie **sags under its own weight** and **vibrates**, which is unsightly, can rattle connections and causes fatigue. It is a favourite question precisely because the reason is not strength.

**Built-up compression members** — two or more sections acting together — need **lacing or battening** so the components behave as one member rather than several independent ones. Lacing is designed for a **transverse shear of 2.5% of the axial load**, and battens for that shear plus the resulting moment. Without them the built-up column's capacity is only the sum of the individual components buckling separately, which is far less.

sections.heading: Connections
sections.body:
Connections are where steel structures actually fail, and where most of the design effort goes.

**Bolted connections — bearing type.** Three checks per bolt, and the capacity is the **least**:

> **Shear: V_dsb = (n_n A_nb + n_s A_sb) f_ub / (√3 × 1.25)**
> **Bearing: V_dpb = 2.5 k_b d t f_u / 1.25**
> **Tension: T_db = 0.9 f_ub A_nb / 1.25**, also limited by f_yb A_sb (γ_m1/γ_m0)/γ_m0

A bolt in **double shear** has twice the capacity of one in single shear, because two shear planes cross it — which is why a **double-cover butt joint** is far more efficient than a single-cover one for the same number of bolts.

**Geometric limits, examined directly:**

| Item | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Minimum pitch** | **2.5 d** |
| **Maximum pitch** | **least of 32 t and 300 mm** |
| **Minimum edge / end distance** | **1.5 × the hole diameter** (rolled edge), 1.7 (sheared edge) |
| **Maximum edge distance** | **12 t ε** |
| Hole diameter | Bolt + 1 to 3 mm clearance depending on size |

The **minimum pitch of 2.5d** exists so the bolts do not tear a common failure path through the plate; the **maximum** exists to prevent the plate buckling between fasteners and to keep the joint tight against corrosion; and the **minimum edge distance** prevents the bolt tearing out through the plate edge.

**High Strength Friction Grip (HSFG) bolts** work differently: they are **pretensioned** so that load is transferred by **friction between the plates**, not by bolt shear and bearing. Consequences:

| HSFG | Bearing-type |
|---|---|
| **No slip** under service load | Slip occurs as the bolt takes up clearance |
| **Better fatigue** performance | Poorer |
| Suits **dynamic loading**, bridges | Suits static loading |
| More expensive; needs controlled tightening | Cheaper, simpler |

The no-slip property is what matters in a bridge or crane girder, where repeated load reversal would work a bearing-type joint loose.

**Welded connections.** The **fillet weld** is the workhorse:

> **Effective throat thickness = 0.7 × size** (for a 90° fillet)
> **Effective length = actual length − 2 × size**
> **Strength = 0.7 s L_eff × f_u / (√3 × γ_mw)**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum size** | Governed by the **THICKER** plate (to avoid rapid cooling and cracking) |
| **Maximum size** | Governed by the **THINNER** plate (0.7 t at a rounded toe) |
| Minimum effective length | **4 × the weld size** |
| End returns | Twice the weld size, around corners |

The minimum/maximum pairing is worth understanding: a **small** weld on a **thick** plate cools too fast and cracks, so the minimum follows the thicker plate; a **large** weld on a **thin** plate burns through and cannot be supported, so the maximum follows the thinner one.

A **butt weld** with full penetration is **as strong as the parent metal**, so no calculation is needed — the design simply matches the plate. Its cost is edge preparation and, for thick plates, multiple passes.

**Weld defects** examined by name: **undercut**, **porosity**, **slag inclusion**, **lack of penetration**, **lack of fusion**, **cracking**, **distortion** and **residual stress**. Inspection is by **visual**, **dye penetrant**, **magnetic particle**, **ultrasonic** and **radiographic** methods — the last two being the ones that reveal **internal** defects.

**Bolts or welds?**

| Bolted | Welded |
|---|---|
| **Site-friendly**, no power or skilled welders needed | Needs skilled labour and power |
| **Dismantlable**; suits temporary and modular work | Permanent |
| No heat distortion | **Distortion and residual stress** |
| **Reduces the net section** (holes) | **Full section effective** |
| Inspection is visual and simple | Needs NDT for confidence |
| Heavier — gussets, splice plates | **Lighter, cleaner** connections |

Current practice is generally to **weld in the shop and bolt on site** — taking the efficiency of welding where conditions are controlled and the simplicity of bolting where they are not. That is also why questions about site connections usually expect bolts.

**Connection types by behaviour:**

| Type | Transmits |
|---|---|
| **Simple (flexible)** | **Shear only** — treated as a hinge |
| **Rigid (moment)** | Shear **and moment** — full continuity |
| Semi-rigid | Partial moment |

The classification matters because the **analysis must match the connection**: designing a frame as rigid and then providing flexible cleats gives a structure with no lateral stiffness, while the reverse gives moments the connection was never designed for.

sections.heading: Beams, plate girders and industrial structures
sections.body:
**Design of a rolled steel beam**, in sequence:

1. Compute the factored **moment and shear**.
2. Estimate the required **Z_p = M_u γ_m0 / f_y** and select a trial section.
3. **Classify** the section.
4. Check the **design bending strength**, including **lateral–torsional buckling** if the compression flange is unrestrained.
5. Check **shear**, and **web buckling and crippling** at supports and concentrated loads.
6. Check **deflection** against the serviceability limit.
7. Check the **bearing** at supports and design stiffeners if needed.

**Deflection limits (IS 800 Table 6):**

| Element | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Floor beam, live load** | **span/300** |
| Floor beam supporting brittle finishes | span/360 |
| **Cantilever** | **span/150** |
| Purlin, sheeting only | span/150 |
| **Crane girder** (manual / electric) | span/500 to span/1000 |
| Column, lateral drift | **height/300** per storey |

The **crane girder's very tight limit** reflects the fact that an out-of-level rail causes the crane to jam or derail — a serviceability requirement with an operational consequence.

**Plate girders** are used where no rolled section is deep enough. Their design is dominated by **web behaviour**, because economy pushes the web to be as thin as possible:

| Element | Function and consideration |
|---|---|
| **Flanges** | Carry almost all the **moment**; sized from M/(f_y d) |
| **Web** | Carries the **shear**; thin, so **buckling** governs |
| **Bearing stiffeners** | Under concentrated loads and at supports, to prevent **crippling** |
| **Intermediate (transverse) stiffeners** | Divide the web into panels, raising its **shear buckling** capacity |
| Longitudinal stiffeners | For very deep webs, resisting bending buckling |

**Tension field action** is the concept that makes thin webs viable: once a web panel buckles in shear, it can still carry load as a series of **diagonal tension bands**, provided the flanges and stiffeners can anchor the resulting forces — like a Pratt truss forming within the panel. IS 800's **post-critical** and **tension field** methods use this, which is why a plate girder web need not be designed to avoid buckling altogether.

**Industrial building components**, examined by name and function:

| Component | Duty |
|---|---|
| **Purlins** | Span between trusses, carrying the sheeting; usually **angles or channels**, checked for **biaxial bending** since the load is normal to the sloping roof |
| **Rafters (principal)** | The inclined truss members, in **compression** |
| **Tie** | The bottom chord, in **tension** |
| **Sag rods** | Support purlins about their weak axis, reducing the effective span |
| **Bracing** | Provides **stability and transfers lateral load** to the foundations |
| **Gantry (crane) girder** | Carries the crane rail; designed for **moving loads with impact** and **lateral surge** |
| **Column base plate** | Spreads the column load onto the concrete foundation |

**Purlins are checked for biaxial bending** because the roof slopes: the vertical load has components **normal to and along** the roof plane, so the purlin bends about both axes. An angle or channel used as a purlin has the further complication that its **shear centre lies outside the section**, so it also **twists** unless restrained — which is why sag rods and cleats matter.

**Bracing deserves emphasis** because it is often treated as an afterthought and is in fact what makes a steel frame stable. It provides the load path for wind and seismic force, prevents the frame from racking, and **reduces the effective length** of compression members. Types: **cross (X) bracing**, **K bracing**, **portal bracing**, and for seismic work **eccentric bracing**, which is deliberately detailed so a short link yields in shear and dissipates energy.

**Column bases:**

| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| **Slab base** | Axial load only; the plate simply spreads the load |
| **Gusseted base** | Larger loads, and where **moment** must be transferred |
| Moment-resisting base | Fixed-base frames; needs holding-down bolts designed for tension |

The base plate area follows from the **bearing strength of the concrete** (0.45 f_ck under IS 800), and the plate thickness from the **bending** induced by the upward bearing pressure on the projection beyond the column. **Holding-down bolts** must be designed for **uplift** where the frame can overturn — the 0.9DL load combination again.

**Corrosion protection** is a serviceability and durability requirement that questions do ask about: **surface preparation (blast cleaning)** first, then **priming** (red lead or zinc-rich), then finishing coats; or **galvanising** for long life in exposed conditions. **Fire protection** is by **encasement in concrete**, **intumescent paint**, or **sprayed fibre**, because unprotected steel loses about **half its strength at 550 °C** — steel's principal disadvantage against concrete, and the reason fire ratings govern the choice of protection system.

formulas.label: Partial safety factors (IS 800)
formulas.expression: γ_m0 = 1.10 (yielding, buckling) ;   γ_m1 = 1.25 (ultimate/rupture) ;   welds 1.25 shop, 1.50 site
formulas.note: Larger factors for brittle modes and for less-controlled conditions.

formulas.label: Tension member capacity
formulas.expression: T_dg = A_g f_y/1.10 ;   T_dn = 0.9 A_n f_u/1.25 ;   plus block shear — take the LEAST
formulas.note: Net-section rupture takes the larger factor because it is brittle. Shear lag reduces single-angle capacity.

formulas.label: Compression member
formulas.expression: P_d = A_e f_cd, with f_cd from the non-dimensional slenderness and buckling class a/b/c/d
formulas.note: Four curves account for residual stresses that differ with shape, axis and manufacturing process.

formulas.label: Design bending strength
formulas.expression: Class 1–2: M_d = β_b Z_p f_y/γ_m0 ;   Class 3: M_d = Z_e f_y/γ_m0 ;   cap 1.2 Z_e f_y/γ_m0
formulas.note: Reduce by χ_LT if the compression flange is laterally unrestrained.

formulas.label: Shear capacity
formulas.expression: V_d = A_v f_yw/(√3 γ_m0),  A_v = web area for a rolled I-section
formulas.note: The √3 comes from von Mises. The web carries about 95% of the shear.

formulas.label: Bolt capacities
formulas.expression: shear V_dsb = (n_n A_nb + n_s A_sb) f_ub/(√3 × 1.25) ;   bearing V_dpb = 2.5 k_b d t f_u/1.25
formulas.note: Double shear gives twice the capacity. Take the least of shear, bearing and tension.

formulas.label: Bolt geometry
formulas.expression: minimum pitch 2.5d ;  maximum least of 32t and 300 mm ;  minimum edge distance 1.5 × hole diameter
formulas.note: Minimum pitch avoids a common tear path; maximum prevents plate buckling between fasteners.

formulas.label: Fillet weld
formulas.expression: throat = 0.7 × size ;  L_eff = L − 2 × size ;  strength = 0.7 s L_eff f_u/(√3 γ_mw)
formulas.note: Minimum size set by the THICKER plate, maximum by the THINNER. Minimum length 4 × size.

formulas.label: Section classification limits
formulas.note: Higher grade steel has TIGHTER limits. Plastic design requires Class 1 only.

formulas.label: Deflection limits (IS 800 Table 6)
formulas.expression: floor beam live load span/300 ; cantilever span/150 ; crane girder span/500–1000 ; drift height/300
formulas.note: The crane girder limit is operational — an out-of-level rail jams the crane.
